subject: pharmacology
title: Pharmacokinetic Drug Redistribution and Area Under the Concentration-Time Curve

steps.tx: The rapid termination of pharmacological effect resulting from the movement of a drug from highly perfused vessel-rich organs to less perfused bulk tissue reservoirs is termed **redistribution**. Rather than hepatic biotransformation or renal excretion, physical diffusion down a concentration gradient terminates the clinical effect. This unique pharmacokinetic phenomenon occurs exclusively with highly lipid-soluble drugs administered rapidly via intravenous injection, most famously exemplified by intravenous general anaesthetics.
steps.say: Redistribution terminates drug action by transferring lipophilic drugs from brain tissue into muscle and adipose depots.

left.title: Redistribution termination
points: Driven by differential tissue blood perfusion
Drug remains intact inside the body
Occurs within minutes after intravenous bolus
Governs recovery after single thiopental bolus

right.title: Metabolic clearance termination
points: Drug is irreversibly destroyed or conjugated
Requires hours to clear systemic drug burden
Governs recovery after prolonged continuous infusion

steps.tx: Intravenous bolus injection of the ultra-short-acting barbiturate thiopental sodium produces immediate loss of consciousness within twenty seconds as high cerebral blood flow rapidly equilibrates the drug into the brain. Over the subsequent five to fifteen minutes, plasma concentrations decline sharply as the drug redistributes into well-perfused skeletal muscle and ultimately into adipose tissue. This rapid tissue translocation causes clinical awakening from **thiopental anaesthesia** despite more than ninety percent of the administered dose still residing in the body.
steps.say: Awakening from thiopental anaesthesia occurs within ten minutes as drug diffuses from the brain into muscle reservoirs.

nodes.label: Vessel-rich brain rapid peak equilibration (<1 min)
Redistribution into intermediate skeletal muscle (5-15 min)
Terminal slow uptake into adipose reservoir
Patient awakens despite 90% body drug burden remaining

steps.tx: While a single intravenous dose of thiopental exhibits a brief duration of action due to rapid redistribution, repeated boluses or prolonged continuous infusions saturate the peripheral skeletal muscle and adipose storage depots. Once tissue storage capacity is exhausted, the concentration gradient driving redistribution collapses, leaving elimination entirely dependent on slow hepatic metabolism. This accumulation markedly prolongs clinical recovery, a concept formalized in anaesthesia as the **context-sensitive half-time**.
steps.say: Repeated doses saturate muscle and fat reservoirs, eliminating redistribution gradients and prolonging recovery dependent on liver metabolism.

right.title: Prolonged continuous infusion
points: Tissue depots fully saturated with drug

steps.tx: Redistribution governs the clinical duration of several other lipophilic central nervous system depressants, including intravenous diazepam and propofol. When intravenous diazepam is administered for status epilepticus, central anticonvulsant activity terminates within thirty minutes due to extensive vascular redistribution into peripheral tissues, necessitating prompt initiation of a long-acting antiepileptic like fosphenytoin to prevent **seizure recurrence**. Propofol similarly displays rapid clinical recovery driven by extensive initial redistribution.
steps.say: Intravenous diazepam redistributes out of the brain within thirty minutes, necessitating longer-acting antiepileptics to prevent seizure recurrence.

steps.tx: The definite integral of plasma drug concentration plotted as a function of time from time zero to infinity represents the **area under the curve**. Designated as AUC, this critical pharmacokinetic metric reflects the total amount of active unchanged drug that reaches the systemic circulation following administration. AUC serves as the gold-standard mathematical foundation for quantifying total body clearance, calculating absolute bioavailability, and demonstrating regulatory bioequivalence between pharmaceutical formulations.
steps.say: Area under the curve measures total systemic drug exposure over time, serving as the basis for clearance and bioavailability.

nodes.label: Derivation of total clearance and bioavailability

steps.tx: Total systemic body clearance is inversely proportional to total drug exposure, determined by dividing the administered intravenous dose by the resultant exposure area. This fundamental mathematical relationship, the **clearance formula**, states that clearance equals dose divided by AUC. When clearance is compromised by hepatic cirrhosis or acute tubular necrosis, total drug clearance declines, causing the plasma concentration-time curve to elevate and AUC to expand proportionately.
steps.say: Systemic clearance equals dose divided by area under the curve, decreasing in organ failure as exposure area expands.

steps.tx: Determining the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation requires comparing extravascular exposure to an identical intravenous dose. The mathematical relationship, designated as the **bioavailability equation**, calculates absolute bioavailability (F) by dividing oral AUC by intravenous AUC, multiplied by the ratio of intravenous dose to oral dose. This calculation allows clinical pharmacologists to evaluate the efficiency of gastrointestinal absorption and determine oral dose equivalencies.
steps.say: Absolute bioavailability compares oral to intravenous area under the curve, adjusting for dose differences.

steps.tx: Pathological alterations in organ function and drug interactions substantially alter the total area under the concentration-time curve, precipitating adverse clinical consequences. Co-administration of a metabolic enzyme inhibitor blunts drug elimination, increasing the terminal half-life and dramatically elevating the **systemic exposure**. Conversely, malabsorption syndromes, diarrhoea, or co-administration of binding resins decrease oral AUC, leading to subtherapeutic drug levels and catastrophic treatment failure in organ transplant recipients.
steps.say: Enzyme inhibition expands systemic exposure area and risks toxicity, whereas malabsorption reduces exposure, causing treatment failure.

right.title: Causes of decreased AUC
points: Bowel resection or short gut syndrome
